study.title: Study of Zephaniah 3
study.overview: Zephaniah 3 alternates denunciation and hope. First, the prophet exposes the corruption of Jerusalem and its leaders, showing that the city, though privileged, rejected correction, trust in the Lord and closeness to his God. Then the chapter broadens the horizon: God's judgment on the nations and on the city itself prepares a restoration in which the people will be purified, humble, secure and reunited again. The end of the chapter presents the Lord as King in the midst of his people, removing fear, shame and oppression, and returning to Israel's name and honor among the peoples.

outline.title: The blame of Jerusalem and the holiness of God
outline.explanation: The text begins with a lament against the oppressive city. The accusation strikes the people and their leaders: princes, judges, prophets, and priests. All fail in basic duties of justice, truth, and fidelity. In contrast, the LORD remains righteous in the midst of it, making the persistence of sin even more serious.

outline.title: The announced judgment and the promise of meeting of the nations
outline.explanation: God remembers what he did with other nations to show that his judgment is real and pedagogical. But Jerusalem did not learn. Even so, the Lord calls for confidence, because the day will come when he will gather peoples and kingdoms to shed indignation upon evil, and then he will grant the people a pure lip to invoke his name and serve him in unity.

outline.title: Purification of the remnant and joy of the divine presence
outline.explanation: The shame linked to pride and infidelity will be removed. God will preserve a humble and poor people who will trust in his name. This remnant will be characterized by truth, peace and security, because the LORD is among him as a warrior who saves, but also as he who rejoices, here and loves his people.

outline.title: Meeting of dispersions and public restoration
outline.explanation: The chapter ends with the promise to gather those who suffer from the absence of the feasts, to end the oppressors and to save the marginalized and expelled. The result will be a complete reversal of shame: the restored people will have renown and praise among all the peoples, because the LORD himself will bring you back and restore it before their eyes.

study.context: The chapter speaks to Jerusalem and Zion as direct targets of rebuke and promises. The setting presupposes a religious and politically responsible city, but corrupted in its leaders and practices. The notes highlight that prophecy is given amid judgment, with the need to wait for God's action. They also suggest that the promised restoration reaches a broad horizon, including the nations, and unfolds into blessings that the text relates to the purified people.
study.theology: Zephaniah 3 presents three central truths. First, God judges with righteousness the corruption of his people and his leaders; religious closeness does not nullify moral responsibility. Second, restoration is the work of divine grace: the Lord not only punishes, but purifies, gathers and transforms, granting a humble, true and secure people. Third, God's presence is the centre of hope: the King of Israel dwells in the midst of his people, removes shame and produces joy, peace and unity. The text also points to the universal dimension of God's work, for peoples and nations are included in the reach of their action, and true worship becomes common among them. In evangelical reading, this holds the conviction that judgment and salvation belong to the same holy God, and that his promise is reliable because he himself declared it.

scholarViews.insight: The day of the LORD culminates, after severe judgment, in lasting blessings for those who trust in him; the prophecy is entirely trustworthy because it was spoken by the LORD Himself.
The chapter goes from the rebuke of Jerusalem's wickedness to the promise of mercy: God first purifies, then saves and restores his people.
The final promise includes the restoration of the people and their honor among the nations; he sees in this outcome a broad horizon of favor and prosperity connected with the divine work.

questions: What forms of empty religiosity and injustice appear in the description of Jerusalem, and how can they appear today in communities of faith?
What does it mean, in practice, to wait for the Lord when the situation seems to worsen rather than improve?
How does the promise of a humble, true and secure people confront our desires by status, control and self-promotion?
study.practice: Examine your life and your community in the light of the leaders of Jerusalem: is there inconsistency between speech and practice, between worship and justice, between trust in God and trust in human resources? Repent from any form of pride or lie, and ask the LORD to form in you a humble heart that trusts in your name. Also practice patient hope: instead of giving in to discouragement, feed your faith with the assurance that God judges evil, purifies his people and restores what has been broken. Seek a concrete attitude of reconciliation, truth and service to those who have been humiliated or excluded.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are limited and do not explain in detail all verses. It is not possible to safely affirm the exact historical context, the date of prophecy, nor to accurately identify how the restoration of 3:20 is fulfilled in all its unfoldings. Some readings in the notes see a Messianic range and even related to the gospel, but this should be treated as an interpretation, not as explicit detail of the text. Nor is there sufficient basis in the notes to define conclusively whether all references to nations and peoples should be read only in an immediate or also eschatological sense.
